name: Chronological snobbery
statement: Chronological snobbery treats an idea as discredited by having gone out of date, without asking whether anyone refuted it or whether it merely fell out of fashion.
meaning: Lewis defines it as "the uncritical acceptance of the intellectual climate common to our own age and the assumption that whatever has gone out of date is on that account discredited". The test he attaches is historical rather than psychological. "You must find why it went out of date. Was it ever refuted (and if so by whom, where, and how conclusively) or did it merely die away as fashions do? If the latter, this tells us nothing about its truth or falsehood." The passage then turns the same suspicion on the present. Lewis writes that our own age is also a period and has, like all periods, its characteristic illusions, and that these are likeliest to lurk in the widespread assumptions so ingrained that nobody attacks or defends them. What is being judged is an argument, not a person. Lewis reports no experiment, names no population and gives no rate, which places chronological snobbery among named fallacies rather than among measured effects. Wiley's fallacy compendium catalogues it under that heading.

origin.where: Surprised by Joy: The Shape of My Early Life
origin.note: The phrase appears in chapter XIII, "The New Look", of the Geoffrey Bles edition published in London in 1955. In that setting the definition, the historical test that follows it and the turn on the present all sit on page 196. Lewis introduces it as "what I have called my 'chronological snobbery'", so the naming is his own. He credits the counter-attacks to Owen Barfield, writing that they "destroyed forever two elements in my own thought", of which this was the first. The dispute he calls the Great War began when Barfield became an anthroposophist. Earlier in the chapter, on page 195, Lewis dismisses anthroposophy as medieval and adds that he still used the names of earlier periods as terms of abuse. Chapter XIV softens the word destroyed. There Barfield is "beginning to overthrow" the attitude, Nevill Coghill gives it another blow, and on page 205 it is "seriously shaken". The text was read in the Distributed Proofreaders Canada transcription of the 1955 Bles printing, which carries the Bles title page and the publisher's 1955 imprint.

evidence: The evidence for chronological snobbery is a passage of autobiography and the tradition of fallacy lists that took the phrase up. There is no study of it, and no measured effect carries the name. Three measured literatures sit next to it, none of them designed to test it, and they do not agree on direction, so none can stand in for it. The newness premium, appeal to novelty at entry 495, runs the way Lewis describes, and the existence and longevity work, appeal to tradition at entry 493, runs the other way. Those entries carry the figures and the replications. The nearest of them to the charge is the second. Eidelman, Crandall and Pattershall report five studies in which mere existence is treated as evidence of goodness. An existing state is rated above an alternative, a form described as more prevalent is judged more aesthetically attractive, and the effect extends to how a food tastes. Their follow-up on duration, titled "Longer is better", was not obtained on any route tried, so nothing is quoted from it here. McCabe, Spina and Arndt describe it as holding "that which exists is good and that which has existed for longer is better", and their own experiment had participants reminded of death evaluate new, 20-year-old and 100-year-old objects, with the death reminders raising the valuation of the older ones. The second literature asks whether scholarship neglects older work, and finds the opposite of neglect. Verstak and colleagues at Google counted citations in articles published between 1990 and 2013. In 2013, 36% of citations went to articles at least ten years old, a share that had grown by 28% since 1990. The fraction rose in seven of nine broad areas of research and in 231 of 261 subject categories, and the increase over 2002 to 2013 was double that over 1990 to 2001. For articles at least 15 years old the 2013 share was 21%, up 30% since 1990, and for those at least 20 years old it was 13%, up 36%. Those figures come from an arXiv preprint by Google employees, and Crossref holds no journal version of it. The third is the treatment of novelty in clinical trials, which is a claim about study design rather than about judging ideas. Tinè, Attanasio, Muggeo and Crainiceanu ran a meta-regression of hepatitis C interferon trials. The same therapy did better when it occupied the experimental arm than when it occupied the control arm, by a mean of 11.9%, p < 0.0001. That unadjusted gap was absent in one of the three interferon groups, and arm type stayed significant at p = 0.0009 once trial and patient characteristics were adjusted for.

replication.headline: No study of chronological snobbery was found. It is a name for a bad argument, and nothing located turns it into a claim about people that could pass or fail.
replication.detail: Searches on 21 September 2026 of Crossref, Europe PMC and arXiv return no empirical work on the phrase. Crossref carries three records with it in the title, all humanities: the chapter in Wiley's Bad Arguments, a chapter in the Inklings yearbook whose record gives no author and no year, and a 2015 article in English21 on the Chronicles of Narnia. Europe PMC holds three records containing the phrase, in pieces on surgical burnout, Canadian medical education and hospital inpatient complexity, and each uses it in passing rather than studying it. An arXiv full-text query returns nothing. Open Library's search inside the Internet Archive's books returns 511 hits, and the ones it ranks first are apologetics and logic primers. The adjacent measurements are not replications, and they point both ways rather than one: see entry 493 and entry 495.

limits: The search covered Crossref by bibliographic query, Europe PMC, arXiv full text, Open Library's search inside the Internet Archive's books, and general web search, all on 21 September 2026. OpenAlex was tried again and still refused, this time naming the reason: the free daily budget shared by everyone on this network's address was spent, and the request carried no API key. No psychology-specific database such as PsycINFO was searched. Absence of a study is therefore a statement about those places and not about the whole literature. Several documents were not obtained. Eidelman, Pattershall and Crandall's 2010 paper is closed at the publisher, and Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE and Europe PMC list no open copy, so everything said about it here comes from McCabe, Spina and Arndt's description. Holdier's chapter in Bad Arguments is cited from its Crossref record, which gives title, book, publisher, pages and date. The chapter itself is not behind a paywall message but behind a Cloudflare interstitial, which is what Wiley served on every attempt. The same interstitial guards the full text of the McCabe paper, so its abstract was used. Wikipedia cites page 164 of Owen Barfield's History in English Words, and the Encyclopedia Barfieldiana entry, read from a 2013 snapshot at the Wayback Machine, quotes that page. The sentence describes the attitude and does not name it, so the citation supports the concept and not the coinage. The book itself stays lending-restricted at the Internet Archive, its plain text file returns a 403, and the archive's full-text search host was refused by this session's egress, so whether Barfield used the phrase in print is still unsettled. The Inklings yearbook chapter titled "C.S. Lewis and Chronological Snobbery" has a Crossref record carrying no author and no year. Of the adjacent literatures only Verstak was read in full; the others were read at abstract level. None of them was designed to test Lewis's claim, and treating any of them as a verdict on it would be a category error.
misreadings: The coinage is routinely given to two people. Wikipedia states that the term "was coined by C. S. Lewis and Owen Barfield" and marks that sentence as needing a citation, dated June 2024. Lewis's own text says "what I have called my 'chronological snobbery'" and credits Barfield with the counter-attacks, not with the name. Page references also drift. Wikipedia quotes the definition from chapter 13, pages 207 to 208, and cites page 206 for the remark about medieval as a term of abuse. The 1955 Bles printing puts the definition on page 196 and that remark on page 195, and later editions repaginate. A second error is to expect an effect size. Chronological snobbery is a charge about the structure of an argument, and no study located has assigned it a rate or a magnitude. A third is to read Lewis as saying old ideas are better. He says that an idea dying away as fashions do tells us nothing about its truth, and he applies the same suspicion to the assumptions of his own age. The fourth is to settle the psychology by picking whichever neighbouring literature is nearest to hand. Work on existence and duration finds older and longer established things rated better, and work on novelty finds the later date preferred and paid for even when it carries no information. Neither was built to test Lewis, and each is set out where it belongs, at entry 493 and entry 495. The last is to merge it with declinism, entry 124, which points the other way. Declinism is a belief that contemporaries are getting worse, and that entry carries the survey record. Chronological snobbery is a belief that past thought is discredited by being past. A single person can hold both, because the objects are different: the conduct of contemporaries in one case, the standing of old arguments in the other.

sources.text: Lewis, C. S. (1955). Surprised by Joy: The Shape of My Early Life. London: Geoffrey Bles. Chapter XIII, "The New Look", page 196, with pages 195 and 205 read for the surrounding claims. Read as the Distributed Proofreaders Canada transcription, Faded Page eBook #20150220, in the PDF copy hosted at orcuttchristian.org, fetched and searched in this session. Source for the definition, the attribution to Barfield and the pagination.
Faded Page (2015). Surprised by Joy: The shape of my early life, eBook #20150220. The catalogue record for the transcription read above, giving 1955, Geoffrey Bles and 241 pages. Read.

Holdier, A. G. (2018). Chronological Snobbery. In Bad Arguments, 311-313. Wiley. Cited for the entry's existence in a fallacy compendium. The chapter was not obtained: Wiley answered every attempt with a Cloudflare interstitial rather than a paywall notice, and the bibliographic details come from its Crossref record, re-resolved on 21 September 2026.

Eidelman, S., Crandall, C. S., & Pattershall, J. (2009). The existence bias. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 97(5), 765-775. Abstract read at Europe PMC, PMID 19857000; full text closed. The five studies are summarised at entry 493, which carries this literature.

Eidelman, S., Pattershall, J., & Crandall, C. S. (2010). Longer is better. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 46(6), 993-998. Not obtained. Retried on 21 September 2026 through Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, CORE, Europe PMC and the first author's laboratory page, none of which holds a copy. Its content is described here from McCabe, Spina and Arndt.

McCabe, S., Spina, M. R., & Arndt, J. (2016). When existence is not futile: The influence of mortality salience on the longer-is-better effect. British Journal of Social Psychology, 55(3), 600-611. Abstract read at Europe PMC, PMID 27041146. Source for the quoted description of the longer-is-better effect and for the design with new, 20-year-old and 100-year-old objects. Full text guarded by a Cloudflare interstitial at Wiley.

Verstak, A., Acharya, A., Suzuki, H., Henderson, S., Iakhiaev, M., Lin, C. C. Y., & Shetty, N. (2014). On the Shoulders of Giants: The Growing Impact of Older Articles. arXiv:1411.0275. PDF fetched and searched in this session; every citation-share figure above was found in it. A preprint: a Crossref title search on 21 September 2026 returned no journal version.

Tinè, F., Attanasio, M., Muggeo, V. M. R., & Crainiceanu, C. M. (2017). Evidence of bias in randomized clinical trials of hepatitis C interferon therapies. Clinical Trials, 14(5), 483-488. Structured abstract read at Europe PMC, PMID 28670909. Source for the 11.9% mean arm difference, for the group with no difference and for the adjusted p value. Full text closed at the publisher.
